clue.text: Some highly coloured dirt staged by

definitions.meaning: taken literally, soil of a rich violet hue
the title of a 1940 comedy by Sean O'Casey, the answer at 27 across

explanation.surface: A gaudily tinted heap of soil is put on stage by somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference number 27 was lost from the printed text; the clue points to the playwright at 27 across, whose comedy of English country life carries this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The two words of the title literally describe vividly coloured grime, and they also name an O'Casey stage comedy.

clue.text: Saint seen as leader by many in Gubbi

definitions.text: Saint seen as leader by many in Gubbi

parts.words: Saint seen as leader by many in Gubbi
parts.note: the printed Gubbi is Gubbio, the Umbrian town whose twelfth-century bishop is its patron saint, honoured each May in the Corsa dei Ceri

explanation.walkthrough: The town's name has lost its final O in print and the letter count is missing; the patron of Gubbio is the bishop Saint Ubald, called by his Italian name.
explanation.definitionFit: Patron saint of Gubbio: the town's people regard this twelfth-century bishop as their heavenly protector.

clue.text: She became a swallow, one summer

definitions.text: She became a swallow, one summer

parts.words: She became a swallow, one summer
parts.note: in the Latin retelling of the Athenian sisters' myth, Pandion's daughter was turned into a swallow; 'one summer' plays on the proverb that one swallow does not make a summer

explanation.surface: A woman turned into a bird one summer.
explanation.walkthrough: Greek versions make her the nightingale and her sister the swallow; Latin poets swapped them, which the clue uses, while 'one summer' echoes the proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovid's tale of the raped princess transformed into a songbird, in the Latin tradition a swallow.

clue.text: Several act badly in Life among the Lowly

definitions.note: a character in the novel whose subtitle is Life among the Lowly, Uncle Tom's Cabin

indicators.note: acting badly means the words are performed wrongly, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A troupe performs poorly in a play about humble folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges SEVERAL and ACT together. Life among the Lowly is the subtitle of Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Eva, the saintly child of Augustine St Clare, is a central figure in Stowe's antislavery novel.

clue.text: Spirits offered by Fouqué (with plenty of water)

definitions.text: Spirits offered by Fouqué (with plenty of water)

parts.words: Spirits offered by Fouqué (with plenty of water)
parts.note: the German Romantic Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué wrote the 1811 novella of a water nymph who gains a soul by marrying; the spirits are watery, not a drink diluted

explanation.surface: A host serves liquor well watered down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits ... with plenty of water' sounds like weak drinks; it means elemental water sprites, the subject of Fouqué's novella.
explanation.definitionFit: Paracelsus named the elemental water sprites thus, and Fouqué's tale made one its heroine.

clue.text: "At once he felt the hollow-beaten mosses And tremble…" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "At once he felt the hollow-beaten mosses And tremble…" (Tennyson)

parts.words: "At once he felt the hollow-beaten mosses And tremble…" (Tennyson)
parts.note: a line from Tennyson's Morte d'Arthur, where a word for a dull heavy sound is missing before 'And tremble'

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap from Tennyson's Arthurian poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in the quotation: in Morte d'Arthur the mosses resound with a dull, heavy blow underfoot.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb describes mosses making a dull muffled sound, as when struck by heavy footsteps.

clue.text: Curious relation at Lawrence's assembly

indicators.note: curious suggests the letters of the next word are odd, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd relative turns up at a gathering at Lawrence's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curious' rearranges RELATION. T. E. Lawrence's collected writings appeared posthumously in 1939 as Oriental Assembly, so the answer completes that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence of Arabia's posthumous miscellany bears this adjective as the first word of its title, Assembly being the second.

clue.text: Scary tale produced with professional collaborator?

definitions.meaning: a frightening yarn about the supernatural
a narrative written by a hired writer who works unseen under someone else's name

explanation.surface: A frightening narrative written with the help of a hired professional.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the first word as a hired, uncredited writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectre tales scare readers; an account by a hired anonymous writer is a spook's narrative in the trade sense.

clue.text: Organ at hotel destination for Reade's' vicar

parts.note: the heart is a bodily organ
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A body part at a hotel is where Reade's clergyman ends up.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade's novel The Cloister and the Hearth sets the church against the home; the fireside is the alternative end for its hero Gerard, who becomes a priest.
explanation.definitionFit: Reade's title pairs monastery and fireside, the two places a clergyman's life might lead.

clue.text: Blousy Huguenot

parts.note: the Protestant rebels of the Cévennes took their name from the camisa, the shirt or smock they wore over their clothes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blousy' points to the shirt the rebels wore; these French Protestants rose against Louis XIV around 1702.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cévenol Protestant insurgents were named for their shirts, hence a shirt-wearing Calvinist.

clue.text: Their work is the last thing you may want to consult

definitions.text: Their work is the last thing you may want to consult

parts.words: Their work is the last thing you may want to consult
parts.note: the alphabetical list of subjects at the back of a book, which readers turn to for references, is compiled by these people

explanation.surface: Some professionals are so tedious nobody wants to ask their advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the last thing you may want' sounds like reluctance; it means the list sits literally last in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Compilers of back-of-book reference lists produce the final section readers look things up in.

clue.text: "… a shoulder of mutton sail; and the — gib'd over the top of the cabin" (Defoe)

definitions.text: "… a shoulder of mutton sail; and the — gib'd over the top of the cabin" (Defoe)

parts.words: "… a shoulder of mutton sail; and the — gib'd over the top of the cabin" (Defoe)
parts.note: from Robinson Crusoe: the missing word is the spar along the foot of a sail that swings across when the boat goes about

explanation.surface: A quotation from Defoe with a nautical gap.
explanation.walkthrough: Gib'd means swung across, as a spar does when a fore-and-aft sail changes sides.
explanation.definitionFit: The horizontal spar holding the foot of a sail swings over the deck when it jibes.

clue.text: Formidable, perhaps, as Hood

definitions.meaning: HMS Formidable was a Royal Navy pre-dreadnought warship of 1898
HMS Hood was a Royal Navy battlecruiser sunk by the Bismarck in 1941

explanation.surface: Something fearsome, like a hooded figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Formidable' and 'Hood' read as an adjective and a cowl; both are names of Royal Navy capital ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Both names belong to heavily armed capital warships of the Royal Navy.

clue.text: Position of churchmen in possibly Celtic eras

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Clergy held office in early Celtic times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges CELTIC and ERAS together.
explanation.definitionFit: Offices or posts held by clergy are their clerical positions.

clue.text: Giraudoux's entr'acte

definitions.meaning: Jean Giraudoux wrote a 1933 comedy of this title
a short musical or dramatic piece performed between acts

explanation.walkthrough: A single Italian word serves both: the title of a Giraudoux play and the interlude between acts.
explanation.definitionFit: Giraudoux's play takes its title from the Italian term for an interlude between acts, a synonym of entr'acte.

clue.text: Still life, with figures

parts.note: not a painting of fruit but motionless living people posed as a scene, as in a theatrical staged picture

explanation.walkthrough: 'Still life' wants a painting genre; it is living actors holding still in a posed group.
explanation.definitionFit: A frozen staged group of performers is a living picture, life held still with human figures.

clue.text: He did a lot of work in ghastly good taste

definitions.text: He did a lot of work in ghastly good taste

parts.words: He did a lot of work in ghastly good taste
parts.note: Ghastly Good Taste (1933) was the first prose book of the future Poet Laureate who championed Victorian architecture

explanation.surface: A prolific worker had appalling yet refined judgement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ghastly good taste' sounds like a verdict on style; it is the title of a 1933 book on English architecture by the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet and architectural writer published Ghastly Good Taste and much else.

clue.text: Book greeting for tragic hero

parts.note: OT, the Old Testament, is a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A volume of salutations for a tragic protagonist.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Moor of Venice is the protagonist of a tragedy.

clue.text: Uriah (Poe) conceivably giving feeling of wellbeing

indicators.note: conceivably suggests the names could be put together in another form, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Dickens villain and an American writer combine to give happiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conceivably' rearranges URIAH and POE together; Uriah Heep is Dickens's character.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is an intense sense of happiness and wellbeing.

clue.text: Venetian barrister's clerk in a corner is saved at last

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits within the following words

explanation.surface: A Venetian lawyer's assistant, cornered, is rescued at the last moment.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice Portia poses as a barrister and her maid poses as her clerk. 'at last' simply adds to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Portia's waiting-woman disguises herself as the lawyer's clerk in the trial scene.

clue.text: Ursa Minor, personified by Pooh

definitions.meaning: the constellation whose Latin name means the lesser she-bear
Winnie-the-Pooh is a small stuffed animal, 'a bear of very little brain'

explanation.surface: A northern constellation brought to life by Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.definitionFit: The constellation's Latin name translates to a small ursine creature, which A. A. Milne's toy also embodies.

clue.text: Theatre piece by Beckett

definitions.meaning: Samuel Beckett wrote a 1963 one-act piece with this one-word title, for three heads in urns

explanation.definitionFit: A stage drama in general, and the exact title of a short Beckett work.

clue.text: Paternal variety acquired by Philip Stanhope and Laertes

definitions.text: Paternal variety acquired by Philip Stanhope and Laertes

parts.words: Paternal variety acquired by Philip Stanhope and Laertes
parts.note: Lord Chesterfield's letters counselled his son Philip Stanhope, and Polonius counsels his son Laertes in Hamlet

explanation.surface: Two sons each got something from their fathers.
explanation.walkthrough: Both sons received fatherly counsel: Chesterfield wrote letters to Philip Stanhope, and Polonius lectures Laertes with 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fathers' counsel and recommendations, the kind of guidance both famous sons received.

clue.text: He deployed great influence in Victorian fiction

definitions.text: He deployed great influence in Victorian fiction

parts.words: He deployed great influence in Victorian fiction
parts.note: the hypnotist in George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby, who controls the singer Trilby by mesmerism

explanation.surface: A man was a powerful force in nineteenth-century novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Du Maurier's Trilby gave English a word for a manipulative controlling figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Du Maurier's mesmerist dominates Trilby's will, and his name now means a controlling manipulator.

clue.text: Some highlights from the studio

parts.note: not best moments of a broadcast but powerful electric lamps used in film studios

explanation.surface: A few best moments taken from a recording session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'highlights' wants best bits of a show; it means bright lamps used on film sets.
explanation.definitionFit: Film studios used carbon-arc lamps, bright lights named after the electric discharge.

clue.text: Rain Zeus produces for one whose reign is paramount

indicators.note: produces suggests the letters are worked into something new, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: The sky god makes it rain for a supreme ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produces' rearranges RAIN and ZEUS together.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal overlord holds paramount sovereignty over vassal states.

clue.text: Type expressing slanted views? (may also show a certain amount of stress)

definitions.text: Type expressing slanted views? (may also show a certain amount of stress)

parts.words: Type expressing slanted views? (may also show a certain amount of stress)
parts.note: sloping letters in printing, used to mark emphasis on a word; 'slanted views' plays on biased opinions

explanation.surface: A kind of person given to biased opinions, and somewhat stressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' and 'slanted views' suggest a biased personality; they mean sloping print, and 'stress' is emphasis it marks.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloping printed letters are a typeface often used for emphasis.

clue.text: Abbey finally rejected him, in spite of Gregorian support

definitions.text: Abbey finally rejected him, in spite of Gregorian support

parts.words: Abbey finally rejected him, in spite of Gregorian support
parts.note: Dublin's Abbey Theatre turned down The Silver Tassie in 1928 though Lady Gregory had backed the Irish dramatist's earlier work

explanation.surface: A monastery expelled a man despite the backing of Gregorian chant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abbey' and 'Gregorian' suggest monks and chant; they are the Abbey Theatre and its co-founder Lady Gregory.
